client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on my university assignments at all — I'll sit down to study and just end up staring at the wall, or I start crying out of nowhere. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is incredibly heavy — losing your grandmother, and then trying to hold yourself together enough to function at university, that's a lot to ask of yourself in the middle of grief. I can hear in the way you're speaking that you're exhausted and hurting, even as you're trying to hold it together by questioning whether this will even help. That doubt makes complete sense, and I want you to know that we're not here to "fix" the loss — we're here to help you find a way to breathe through it, one small step at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I mean, when you put it that way, it does feel like a lot. I've been so focused on just getting through each day that I haven't really let myself acknowledge how much I'm actually carrying. But I still don't know if talking about it is going to change anything — like, she's still gone, and my deadlines are still there, and I don't see how sitting here changes that.
therapist: Your voice tells me something important — there's a softness and a kind of quiet exhaustion underneath your words, like you're running on empty even as your mind keeps pushing forward with the "what's the point" questions. That thought — *talking won't change the facts* — is completely understandable, but it's worth gently examining: while talking can't bring her back or erase your deadlines, it can change how much weight you're carrying alone, and that shift can make the difference between drowning and staying afloat. You've already taken a step by naming how much you're holding — that's not nothing, that's actually the beginning.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but I keep thinking, okay, so I talk about it, and then what? The deadlines are still there, the empty apartment is still there, and I still have to figure out how to get through a Thursday that used to mean she'd call me just to check in. I guess I'm just not sure how much lighter I can actually feel when the thing making me heavy isn't going anywhere.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, like the words are tumbling out under pressure — tells me that Thursday detail isn't just a detail, it's a wound, and I don't want to rush past it. You're right that the grief isn't going anywhere, and I'd never promise you "lighter" means the loss stops mattering — but what CBT can help with is loosening the grip of the thoughts that pile *on top* of the grief, like "I should be functioning better" or "this will never get easier," which are adding weight to weight. What if, just for today, we started there — not with fixing the loss, but with noticing what your mind is telling you about yourself *because* of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess... yeah, Thursday is when it really hit me that he was gone, and I've been carrying that day around like evidence of something I did wrong. And I hear what you're saying about the thoughts piling on top of the grief, that actually makes a strange kind of sense to me. But I'm worried that if I start picking apart what my mind is telling me, I'll just find more reasons to feel guilty, not less.
therapist: The way you said that — quickly, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me that guilt has been sitting very close to the surface, waiting. I want to gently pause on something important: you said Thursday feels like "evidence of something you did wrong" — and that's exactly the kind of thought we'd want to look at together, not to dismiss it, but to ask *what is the actual evidence, and is your mind being a fair witness to you right now?* Picking apart these thoughts isn't about finding more reasons to feel guilty — it's about testing whether the guilt is telling you the truth, or whether it's grief in disguise.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that the guilt is just... grief wearing a mask. But another part of me keeps coming back to this feeling that if I had just called him more, or visited that last month when I kept putting it off, maybe things would have felt more resolved between us. It's hard to separate "testing the thought" from just finding new ways to excuse myself for not being there enough.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're saying something so painful, tells me this isn't you making excuses — this is someone who loved their grandmother deeply and is holding that love alongside real regret, which is one of the most human and heartbreaking combinations there is. I want to gently offer this distinction: *testing* the thought isn't about excusing yourself, it's about asking whether you were truly a neglectful grandchild, or whether you were a busy, imperfect human who didn't know that last month was the last month — because nobody ever does. The standard you're holding yourself to — that you should have known, should have done more — is one you'd never apply to someone else you loved, and that gap is worth noticing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it. But there's this voice in my head that keeps saying, "other people manage to call their grandparents every week, other people make the time," and I don't know how to argue against that. It feels like testing the thought is just... finding a clever way to let myself off the hook for something I genuinely did wrong.
therapist: The softness in your voice, even while saying something so harsh about yourself, tells me this comparison — "other people call every week" — is hitting you somewhere very deep and quiet. I want to ask you something gently: do you actually know that other people call every week, or is your grieving mind selectively gathering evidence to build a case against you, the way grief sometimes does? Testing that thought isn't letting yourself off the hook — it's asking whether you're being sentenced by a fair jury, or one made up entirely of your worst fears about yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... I don't actually know that for certain. It's more like I see my cousin posting about visiting my aunt on social media, or I hear my mom mention offhand that someone else checked in, and my brain just runs with it and turns it into this verdict about who I am as a person. But even hearing you say "fair jury" — part of me still feels like the evidence against me is real, because my dad did die and I wasn't calling more, and that's just... a fact I can't reframe my way out of.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, quickly, like you were bracing for impact — tells me something just shifted, because you named something important: your dad. I want to make sure I'm with you fully here, because it sounds like this grief may be carrying more than your grandmother, and I don't want to move past that without acknowledging it. You're right that the facts are real — but the question we haven't asked yet is what those facts say about your *worth as a person*, versus what they say about being someone who was already carrying an enormous amount of pain.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I didn't expect you to catch that — the way I said it, I mean. I've gotten pretty good at slipping things in quietly and hoping nobody notices, and then when someone does notice it kind of knocks the wind out of me. I guess I've been telling myself that my dad leaving is just... a fact, like the weather, but the way you're framing it makes me wonder if I've been using "it's just facts" as a way to avoid asking what it actually means about me.
therapist: The way you said that — quickly, your voice pitched high and tight, like something just cracked open a little — tells me that being noticed landed somewhere very tender and very real. What you just named is genuinely important: "it's just facts" can be a way of protecting yourself from the deeper, scarier question underneath, which might sound something like *"what does it mean about me that my dad left?"* — and that question, I imagine, has been living very quietly and very heavily inside you for a long time. You don't have to answer it all at once, but I want you to know that we've just found something worth sitting with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hate that you're right about that. Like, I've spent so long telling myself it doesn't matter, it's just something that happened, but hearing you say it out loud like that made my chest feel really tight. I don't even know if I want to look at what it means, because part of me is scared that if I start pulling at that thread, I won't be able to stop.
therapist: The tightness in your chest right now is real and important — your body is telling you something your mind has been carefully guarding for a very long time, and that takes courage to sit with even for a moment. I want you to know that pulling at that thread doesn't mean unraveling — it means, slowly and safely, starting to understand the weight you've been carrying so quietly that even you learned not to notice it. We go at your pace, and you're not alone in this.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and part of me really wants to believe it... but there's also this voice in my head that says I've been "going at my own pace" for years and nothing actually changes. Like, what if the weight I'm carrying is just... me? What if it's not something I can put down, but just who I am now? That thought honestly scares me more than the tightness in my chest does.
therapist: The way you said that — your voice pitched high and careful, like you were saying something you've never quite let yourself say out loud before — tells me that thought, *"what if this is just who I am now,"* is one of the loneliest and most frightening things a person can believe about themselves. I want to gently offer this: that thought is not a revelation about your identity, it's actually a very understandable conclusion that a mind draws when it's been carrying pain alone for long enough that the pain and the person start to feel like the same thing. They're not the same thing — and the fact that it *scares* you tells me that somewhere inside, you don't fully believe it either.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
